title: A School for the Study of Life under the Sea. (Naples Aquarium.)
author: ELEANOR HODGEN PATTERSON
first_words: But one room of the beautiful building devoted to the zoölogical station,
last_words: see, so entirely hidden was it behind these many waving, armlike mouths.
why_good: A first-person field observation built on a deliberate illusion and its reversal. The narrator first reads the tank as a garden ('aster', 'cacti', 'chrysanthemums') and then, at feeding time, finds the 'petals' are mouths and the flowers are flesh-eating animals. A careful reader has to track how the writer's interpretation changes and why: the theater and stage-lighting images, the confident quoted guess, the 'kind of shock'. The writer's stance is a delighted, slightly unsettled wonder, and the passage ends on what she still could not see.
suitability: Read the whole article (lines 4372-4597). It covers the public tank room (sea anemones, sea horses, tube worms, jellyfish, octopus fed crabs, cuttlefish ink) and then the upper research floors and how the station is funded. Nothing about race or people beyond scholars, fishermen and a keeper. The anemones are fed raw meat ('sucked in the blood of the meat'), which is mild predation, not cruelty. Later in the article (outside the excerpt) octopi seize crabs the keeper has probably stunned, and specimens are 'killed by powerful chemicals' for preservation. Both are brief and clinical. No numbers inside the excerpt except 'about thirty tanks'.
fame: Eleanor Hodgen Patterson is an otherwise unrecorded contributor, with no other known publications. Original Popular Science Monthly article, not a reprint. The Naples Stazione Zoologica is a real, famous place, but this lay visitor's account of it is obscure.

title: Unusual Forms in Plants.
author: BYRON D. HALSTED
first_words: The influence of moisture, heat, and light is very great upon vegetation,
last_words: monstrous in size and in many cases have lost their essential structure as seed-producing organs.
cuts: Line 3762 only: the caption line '[Illustration: FIG. 3.--A TWIN-FLOWERED CYPRIPEDIUM ACAULE (AIT.).]' sits between paragraphs and is dropped. No prose is omitted.
why_good: An argument with a real turn. Having described 'freaks' found in wild plants, the botanist claims that the garden, the orchard and the county-fair hall are 'all dealing with monstrosities': cultivated watermelons, navel oranges, cauliflower and kohlrabi are as abnormal as any wild sport, and man has shaped them 'to his liking, and not for service to the plant species'. The reader must work out what 'monstrous' means here (not ugly, but departed from the natural type) and see the irony that the deformities we value most are the ones on our dinner plates. The tone is wry and admiring at once.
suitability: Read the whole article (lines 3602-3893): albino wildflowers, green daisies, a twin-flowered lady's slipper, a monstrous foxglove strain. No racial or social content. One phrase outside the excerpt mentions 'vile weeds that have gone West with the advance of civilization' (about weeds, not people). The species name Lobelia syphilitica appears once, outside the excerpt. An opening aside declines to discuss animal abnormalities as 'painful'. No cruelty. The excerpt has no numbers.
fame: Byron D. Halsted (Rutgers botanist and New Jersey station plant pathologist) is known only to historians of plant pathology, not a widely read or taught name. Original Popular Science Monthly article, not a reprint.

title: The Herds of the Yellow Ant.
author: JAMES WEIR, JR., M. D.
first_words: As far as my observations go, and they extend through a period
last_words: objects does not seem to me, therefore, at all wonderful or extraordinary.
cuts: Lines 3029-3044 omitted (two paragraphs on aphid reproduction): from 'If a colony of aphides be kept under observation during' to 'females are born; these mate and the females lay eggs.'

Lines 3056-3249 omitted (egg-gathering, white aphides, ichneumon flies, aphis-lions, lace-wings; contains five [Illustration] lines): from 'In autumn, as soon as ovipositing has begun, the ants' to 'above its head on the tips of the other stalks!'
why_good: The kept portion has three parts. It sets up the ant-and-aphid 'dairy' (ants stroke aphids with their antennae to 'milk' a honey-like fluid). It then reaches the real point: the author openly disputes the eminent Lubbock, who held that the yellow ant will not drop voluntarily from a height. He backs this with a field observation of black-ant raiders and yellow-ant reinforcements dropping from an overhanging leaf, and ends with his own explanation of how the habit could be learned. The reader must separate observation from inference and follow a civil but firm disagreement with an authority ('Lubbock to the contrary notwithstanding').
suitability: Read the whole article (lines 3016-3279). It is natural history of ants, aphids and their insect enemies, with no human or racial content. The omitted middle describes ichneumon larvae feeding inside living aphids. That is ordinary parasitism, briefly and unsensationally described, and it is not in the excerpt. One mild domestic aside compares an aphid to a bedbug. In the excerpt the only number is 'a period of twenty years'.
fame: James Weir Jr. (Owensboro, Kentucky physician, author of 'The Dawn of Reason', 1899) is a minor, little-read figure. Original Popular Science Monthly article, not a reprint. Lubbock is named in the text only as the authority being disputed, which is part of the passage's substance.

title: Development of the American Newspaper.
author: WALTER L. HAWLEY, OF THE NEW YORK EVENING SUN.
first_words: During the first forty years of the present century there was no
last_words: of great events before the full report can be put in type.
why_good: A single self-contained paragraph-run on how news reached early American newspapers. There were no paid reporters: stagecoach drivers, river captains, peddlers and traveling missionaries told what they had heard, and editors printed it laced with their own opinions. The Mexican War is the turning point, showing that readers wanted 'early and complete information' rather than 'individual opinions', and the village post-office reading is the humble origin of the newspaper bulletin board. The reader must infer the author's view that opinion-mixed reporting was a weakness, and grasp the cause-and-effect turn from opinion journals to news. 'The present century' is the nineteenth, which is inferable from the 1812 and Mexican War references.
suitability: Read the whole article (lines 1811-2368): a history of presses, editors, the party press, telegraph, wire services and modern newsrooms. No racial or demeaning content. The excerpt mentions 'Indian uprisings' and 'the subsequent Indian wars' only as kinds of events that got reported, with no characterization of anyone. No cruelty. There are no tables, and the excerpt has no figures beyond 'forty years' and named wars.
fame: Walter L. Hawley was a working New York Evening Sun journalist, not a known writer. Original Popular Science Monthly article, not a reprint.

title: Bookworms in Fact and Fancy.
author: WILLARD AUSTEN.
first_words: So much mystery has gathered around the term bookworm, so much imagery
last_words: its figurative and literal sense, that its misuse will no doubt continue.
cuts: Lines 4156-4218 omitted (classical and Renaissance references: Evenus, Aristotle, Horace, Ovid, Pliny, Martial, Lucian, Pierre Petit; includes a quoted verse): from 'Insects injurious to books and bindings are not a new' to '"impudent creatures" in a thirty-four-line Latin poem titled In Blattam.'
Lines 4235-4245 omitted (Robert Hooke's Micrographia paragraph): from 'The earliest observations on the subject possessing any scientific value' to 'the library as well as other parts of the house.'
why_good: A history-of-an-idea essay. It explains how the 'bookworm' became a half-mythical creature, how earnest searchers (including a 17th-century naturalist who claimed to hear one crow like a cock) kept hunting for one 'genuine bookworm', and the turn that no worm is involved at all: over thirty species of beetles, moths, silverfish, roaches and others do the damage, so 'the term bookworm is a misnomer.' The reader must follow the author's gently ironic stance toward credulous collectors and see the gap between a word's literary life and the facts.
suitability: Read the whole article (lines 4129-4528): classical allusions, then a survey of book-damaging insect groups and their feeding habits. No racial or demeaning content. One line outside the excerpt mentions a dinner party falling through a termite-weakened floor, with no injuries described. A librarian crushes a specimen with his thumb in the excerpt, which is harmless. The excerpt has no measurements, apart from 'eleven different groups', 'over thirty different species' and 'eighteen years'.
fame: Willard Austen was a Cornell University librarian with no literary reputation. Original Popular Science Monthly article, not a reprint. The epigraph is by the obscure Robert Rockliff and is not part of the excerpt.

author: M. HENRI DE PARVILLE.

last_words: to Biarritz. That is the reason a stone is missing at Abbadia.

Lines 3371-3389 omitted (the planned star-catalogue work, the château's architecture and observatory; ends with an [Illustration] line at 3389): from 'The Château of Abbadia will therefore be devoted to the' to 'The interior decoration is very beautiful. [Illustration: FIG. 2.--PRINCIPAL ENTRANCE TO THE CHÂTEAU D'ABBADIE.]'
why_good: A portrait of a person and a place in three beats. The first is a child's 'what is beyond the river? ... I will go and see', which sets up a lifelong curiosity. The second is an old man giving his château to the Academy of Sciences on a single condition: a 50-year catalogue of half a million stars. The third is the deliberately missing balcony stone, kept for a promise Napoleon III made and could never keep after 1870. The reader must connect the anecdotes into a character, infer why the empty space is kept, and read the quiet irony of the closing line.
suitability: Read the whole piece (lines 3282-3449, both gifts). In the omitted part d'Abbadie lived in Ethiopia 'the life of the natives' and mastered five dialects. That is respectful, with no hierarchy, but it uses the dated place-name 'Gallaland'. It is outside the excerpt. The second half (the Duc d'Aumale and Chantilly) mentions his 'tragic death' in the 1897 Bazar de la Charité fire in one clause, without detail. No cruelty. The excerpt has a few figures (310 hectares, 40,000 francs, 500,000 stars, fifty years), no tables.
fame: REPRINT: the closing line reads 'Translated for the Popular Science Monthly from articles in La Nature' (Paris), c. 1897. Henri de Parville was a French science popularizer, unknown to US readers. D'Abbadie is obscure outside Basque and Ethiopian studies. Ranked last for being a translation. An original-article alternative is Ernest A. Lesueur, 'Electricity from Thales to Faraday' (pg47024.txt lines 4051-4091, opening three paragraphs on the 'Edison invented electricity' misconception and the 2,200-year gap after amber). It is not used because the whole article later quotes 'the mangled limbs of frogs' (Galvani) and describes horses driven into electric-eel ponds.
